source.title: SAE features for refusal and sycophancy steering vectors

page_placements.theme: Sparse local supports and task-dependent direction decompositions

record.tranche_reason: It uses SAE feature extraction and steering in language models to test whether dictionary features can recover interpretable, behavior-relevant components, using a different method from the original toy-model study.
record.gate_note: The study also reports SAE training details, quantization results, and MELBO experiments. Training details and quantization results do not test the listed claim versions; MELBO findings are not included because they concern vectors induced to produce varied outputs rather than the claim versions' stated phenomena.
record.test_reason: The study uses SAEs as a tool to decompose refusal, sycophancy and MELBO steering vectors in Phi-3 Mini and Gemma. It reports how well its sparse reconstructions steer behaviour and how well single features classify answers. It does not measure whether real models spread features across neurons or whether SAEs recover a model's sparse features. It also reports no reconstruction or faithfulness metric framed as evidence of superposition. Its results concern this steering-decomposition method's performance, not whether any claim version holds.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors find that gradient pursuit decomposes steering vectors into interpretable features. The Phi-3 refusal reconstruction matched or exceeded the original vector and neared the skyline, but they caution it may not be robust (one judge, 100 samples, SVD-derived vector). Sycophancy results were mixed and failed on Gemma and Gemma 2. The MMLU classifier result did not replicate on TruthfulQA. They call the MELBO results weak and say they are unlikely to continue this direction.
record.recipe_differences: The study applies SAE feature extraction and gradient pursuit to LLM steering vectors; it does not train toy networks with more sparse features than dimensions or measure superposition geometry.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes differed by vector/task and model: refusal reconstruction results varied with the number of SAE features; sycophancy reconstruction was less effective and did not reproduce in Gemma or Gemma 2; classifier strength was weaker on TruthfulQA than MMLU.

fits_no_version.finding: In Phi-3 Mini, a refusal steering direction could be reconstructed from a few SAE features (2–4) without losing steering effect or MMLU. Sycophancy vectors in Gemma and Gemma 2 could not be reproduced by any sparse feature combination the authors found.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Behaviour-relevant steering vectors in LLMs decompose into a small number of SAE dictionary features.

fits_no_version.finding: A single SAE feature taken from a sycophancy-vector decomposition picks the correct MMLU answer 56.1% of the time, but this does not replicate on TruthfulQA.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Individual SAE features from steering-vector decompositions encode transferable task-relevant information such as answer correctness.

record.problems: The refusal evaluation uses just one model and 100 samples, according to the authors; it uses a refusal vector derived from a questionable SVD procedure and reports detailed scores only in charts. Several other findings are qualitative, and uncertainty estimates are not stated.

untested.parts: All: no toy models, sparsity transition or geometry.
All: no analysis of neuron polysemanticity or capacity competition.

No measure of features spread across neurons or of SAE recovery of model features. SAEs are only used to decompose steering vectors; variance explained (74.5%/77.6%) appears only as a quantization training detail.
No test of completeness, stability or canonicity of SAE features.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked all rows to V4 and gave supports/limits_scope labels. However, the study never tests whether LLMs contain sparse features an SAE can recover; it presupposes this and evaluates a steering-decomposition method, so the study is reclassified as T4 and no labels are given. The Gemma and Gemma 2 rows rest on a single sentence. This is a blog post on Alignment Forum/LessWrong, not peer-reviewed.

versions.untested_parts: Toy-model feature superposition, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise from limited capacity and feature competition.
Whether polysemanticity can arise without capacity pressure.
The study tests SAE feature recovery and behavior-related use in selected models and tasks, not how broadly features are distributed across neurons in LLMs.
Whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units.
Whether superposed features are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional features.

rows.subject: Phi-3 Mini
rows.stage_stated: Pretrained on instruction-like data; not finetuned for instruction following
rows.operation_detail: Steered with an SAE reconstruction of the refusal direction using k=4 features.
rows.baseline: Original refusal vector; optimized refusal vector used as a skyline
rows.value: The k=4 reconstruction had better overall performance than the other SAE feature counts and was close to the skyline; the text also says a two-feature SAE reconstruction did not ruin results and could improve the direction.
rows.note: The post refers to charts for the detailed results but gives no numerical refusal or safety scores in the text.
rows.check: Measures steering and safety performance of an SAE reconstruction of a refusal vector, not superposition or SAE recovery of model features; this is the study's own method compared with the original vector and a skyline. The text is inconsistent: it says the direction was reconstructed with two features, then says k=4 performs best. Scores appear only in charts, judged by one guard model on 100 samples, and the authors say the results may not be robust.

source_check.correct: Operation: refusal-direction ablation, projecting the direction out of the residual stream at all layers, rather than activation addition. Layer 16 identifies the SAE used for reconstruction. Refusal is measured using phrases; safety uses locally run LLaMA Guard 2. The k=4 reconstruction has better overall performance and approaches the optimized skyline. State: cannot_determine for the catalog claim; this is the method's performance, linked to no version.
source_check.locator_found: Refusal, lines 44–46; Evaluating vectors and reconstructions, lines 60–68.
source_check.problem: The operation is incorrectly recorded as addition; the observed state describes method performance rather than a claim-version effect.

relation.reason: SAE feature decomposition is used as a tool for interpreting and reproducing steering vectors; reconstruction success or failure does not directly measure superposition or establish dictionary completeness, stability, or canonicality.

tranche.reason: The study applies SAE dictionaries and gradient pursuit to steering-vector reconstruction and reports its method's behavioral and capability performance; these results do not directly test the catalog claim versions.

source_check.notes: The authors' conclusion is consistent with the text; refusal results carry explicit robustness caveats: an SVD-derived direction, one safety judge, and 100 samples. R4 and R5 share one sentence of evidence, with no separate model-specific scores.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Phi-3 Mini refusal-vector reconstruction and MMLU answer classification
reader_labels.reason: SAE reconstructions were reported to preserve or improve refusal-direction performance without sacrificing MMLU, and an individual SAE feature classified MMLU answers at 56.1% accuracy (R1, R2, R6).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Sycophancy features across steering settings and datasets/models
reader_labels.reason: The sycophancy reconstruction was less effective than the original, the features were much weaker on TruthfulQA, and sparse reconstructions failed to reproduce the effect in Gemma and Gemma 2 (R3, R4, R5, R7).
